scope: How a delivery team identifies, records, reviews, responds to and closes project risks and open concerns: the risk register (or RAID log) and its fields, the owner and raiser of each risk, its review cadence, the response options and how one is chosen, and when a risk becomes an issue. Issue severity and triage belong to issue-tracking, and linking in general belongs to project-record-linking; only what a risk record itself carries is researched here. Apple, Android and Windows have no bearing on this topic.
research_type: How-to / troubleshooting (domain project risk management; Product / how-to / definitional LOW-MEDIUM bar, no Statistical claims found)

questions.text: Best practices: what is current best practice for this topic?
Known solutions: what solutions, patterns, libraries and tools already exist, and how do they compare?
Platform guidelines: what do the platform owners' own guidelines say, for each platform the topic touches (Apple, Android, Windows, web, the databases and runtimes concerned)?
The expert's view: if we hired an expert consultant in this topic, what would they tell us: what to do, what to avoid, and what people usually get wrong?

methodology.method: guidelines/researching/process/research-methodology-and-sources: orient, go to the standards bodies and method owners first (ISO 31000, PRINCE2, PMI's PMBOK Guide, HM Treasury's Orange Book, the Scrum and Kanban Guides) and the trackers' own documentation (GitHub, Linear, Atlassian), corroborate across independent publishers, use practitioner sources only where no primary covers the point, record provenance at generation time.
methodology.search_strategy: WebSearch for each standard's and method owner's own text on risk registers, owners, review and responses, and for each tracker's documentation of risk or health fields; every cited page fetched with WebFetch or curl, PDFs read with pdftotext, and each quote checked against the fetched text.
methodology.inclusion: Primary sources: ISO 31000:2018, PRINCE2 2017, PMI's published PMBOK 8 errata, HM Treasury's Orange Book, the UK National Audit Office's good-practice guide, the Scrum Guide, the Kanban Guide, GitHub Docs, Linear Docs, Atlassian's guides. Secondary sources (ILX Group's PRINCE2.com article, the Open Practice Library ROAM page, a Substack summary of PMBOK 8) only where no fetchable primary covered the point, flagged in trust basis.
methodology.exclusion: Search-result snippets, community forum posts, pages that could not be fetched (iso.org OBP, PMI learning library and projectmanagement.com, axelos.com, the SAFe framework site, Jira Align documentation), and any claim not backed by a fetched quote.
methodology.scoring: guidelines/researching/evidence/verification-and-trust-scoring: Authority 30 + Independent corroboration 25 + Accuracy 20 + Currency 10 + Transparency 15, capped by the How-to / Product LOW-MEDIUM bar; secondary sources and copies hosted by third parties score lower.

summary: All five listed rules hold at SHOULD strength. ISO 31000, PRINCE2 and the Orange Book all have teams identify risks early and from anyone, record them in a register whose entries carry an author (raiser), a status and a reference to the product they concern, evaluate each to decide whether action is needed now or the risk is kept under watch, and review the register on a planned basis so nothing goes stale. The topic is missing: a single named owner per risk (with an actionee for the response), a set review cadence (stage boundaries or a fixed interval such as monthly), response triage across avoid, reduce, transfer, share, accept, contingent plans and escalation chosen by cost against tolerance, escalation of risks that exceed tolerance, a risk description written as cause, event and effect, and the hand-over to issue-tracking once a risk has happened. None of the trackers (GitHub, Jira, Linear) ships a dedicated risk record; teams build one from custom issue types and fields or use a project health flag.
open_questions: Which review cadence the rule names: PRINCE2 ties formal review to stage ends and progress reviews, the NAO example is monthly, and the Kanban Guide allows continuous or fixed-interval review; the owner decides whether the rule names one interval or requires the team to set one.

Which response vocabulary the cookbook adopts: ISO 31000's treatment options, PRINCE2's avoid, reduce, transfer, share, accept and prepare contingent plans, PMBOK 8's mitigate, avoid, transfer, accept and escalate, or the ROAM categories (resolved, owned, accepted, mitigated).
Whether opportunities (positive risks) are in this topic's scope: ISO 31000, PRINCE2 and PMBOK 8 all treat them alongside threats, while the listed rules speak only of concerns.
Whether the rule requires a separate actionee beside the owner, as PRINCE2 does, or lets one person hold both, which PRINCE2 says is common.

Which tracker mapping the cookbook recommends for a small team: a custom 'Risk' issue type with fields in GitHub or Jira, a RAID log document, or a project health flag such as Linear's 'At risk', which marks a project but is not a per-risk record.
limitations: ISO 31000:2018 was read from a copy hosted by a university, not from iso.org (its Online Browsing Platform returned 403); PRINCE2 2017 was read from a copy hosted by a university mirror, not from AXELOS.
The PMBOK Guide Eighth Edition core text is paywalled; PMI's own public errata and a secondary Substack summary stand in for it, and the Substack claims are scored as secondary.
ISO 21502 was not fetched and is not cited.

The SAFe framework site and axelos.com are JavaScript-rendered and returned no text; ROAM is cited from the Open Practice Library instead. LeSS was not found to speak to risk registers and is not cited.
Jira Align's risk documentation could not be reached; community posts describing its required risk fields were not fetched in full and are not cited. Jira coverage is Atlassian's own guides.
No study, survey or metric on risk review cadence or register outcomes was found, so no claim takes the Statistical bar; the NAO's monthly review is one organisation's example, not a measured result.
Apple, Android and Windows have no bearing on this topic and were not researched.
Nearly every claim rests on one publisher's words; corroboration is shown by several independent claims under the same verdict rather than by shared wording.
